<!---
I lead the QIS group at IF-NU. Broadly, we ask two linked questions: how do you show an information-processing device is capable of something beyond classical reach — and once you suspect it is, how do you check that claim using only classical means of inference? The first leads to **quantum computational advantage schemes** (sampling-based protocols, fermionic linear optics); the second to **verifying quantum states and processes**, and learning algorithms trained on measurement statistics, using as few trusted qubits as possible.

A third, more foundational thread: the physical world is built out of indistinguishable particles — bosons and fermions — and we're particularly interested in the computational power and verifiability of fermionic systems. Phase-space representations, the natural language for describing bosonic systems (and, with more care, fermionic ones), run through much of this work as a common tool.
--->

::: {.qis-theme-text}
### Quantum computational advantage

::: {.theme-keywords}
[Sampling advantage]{.tag-inline} [Fermionic linear optics]{.tag-inline} [Driven many-body systems]{.tag-inline} [Variational quantum circuits]{.tag-inline} [Phase transitions]{.tag-inline}
:::

How do you show that an information-processing device is doing something beyond classical reach? We build sampling-based advantage schemes—proposals in which a quantum device produces an output distribution provably hard to reproduce classically. One of them, Fermion Sampling, carries average-case hardness guarantees on the same footing as random circuit sampling, and can be certified indirectly, by efficiently learning the fermionic-linear-optical circuit that produced the output samples. We also ask what anti-concentration, a necessary ingredient of such proof, implies about expressivity and trainability of variational quantum models.
<!---We also ask what the ingredients of such proofs imply beyond hardness. Anticoncentration, in particular, bears on the expressivity and trainability of variational quantum models, and distinguishes phases of matter.--->

::: {.qis-theme-text}
### Quantum estimation and certification

::: {.theme-keywords}
[Quantum tomography]{.tag-inline} [Certification]{.tag-inline} [Stabilizer states]{.tag-inline} [Fermionic Gaussian states]{.tag-inline} [Markov chains]{.tag-inline}
:::

With the potential of quantum information processing comes the challenge of verifying that the quantum devices indeed give the correct results. We design measurement strategies and estimators that pin down a state or a process from as few copies and as few trusted assumptions as possible, with provable guarantees on how the sample cost scales. Our recent work certifies fermionic Gaussian states, important reference states for quantum simulations of electronic structure and many-body physics, in a highly efficient manner. 
<!---Once you suspect a device is doing something quantum, how do you check that claim using only classical means of inference — and how efficiently? We design measurement strategies and estimators that pin down a quantum state or process using as few copies, and as few trusted assumptions, as possible, with guarantees on how the precision scales: optimal protocols for verifying that a state was prepared correctly, and estimators whose accuracy is provably as good as the physics allows, from finite-dimensional stabilizer states to the continuous-variable world of fermionic Gaussian states.--->
